`marginplyr` applies one Grouping plan — the ordered list of grouping sets that
the Grouping specification written in `.grouping`, such as
`rollup(region, store)`, expands to — to local data frames and supported lazy
tables. With a database table, the plan remains lazy: `show_query()` renders
the SQL, while `collect()` executes it and brings the result into R.

If grouping sets are new to you, read [Get
started](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/get_started.html)
first. This guide focuses on query shape, execution, and backend support.

## Installation

Install marginplyr from GitHub:

```{r}
#| eval: false

install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("sayuks/marginplyr")

# Used for the optional backend sections of this guide.
install.packages(c("DBI", "duckdb", "RSQLite", "dtplyr", "arrow"))
```

```{r setup}
#| message: false

library(marginplyr)
library(dplyr)
```

Nothing beyond marginplyr's own dependencies is required. The DuckDB, SQLite,
dtplyr, and Arrow sections below need optional packages, so their chunks
evaluate only when those packages are installed at the versions marginplyr asks
for. Where a package is missing or too old the code is still shown, but its
output is absent.

```{r}
#| include: false

# Base R translates its own diagnostics, and a rejected call shows them, so
# the page carries English whatever locale it is rendered in.
Sys.setenv(LANGUAGE = "en")

# `marginplyr_suggest_available()` answers what a bare installation check
# could not: whether the installed package satisfies the version DESCRIPTION
# requires. AGENTS.md is authoritative for which guards must go through it.
source(system.file("suggests", "guard.R", package = "marginplyr"))

has_duckdb <- marginplyr_suggest_available("DBI") &&
  marginplyr_suggest_available("duckdb")
# dbplyr's SQLite simulator opens no connection, but rendering its SQL reads
# the installed driver version through RSQLite.
has_sqlite_simulator <- marginplyr_suggest_available("RSQLite")
# The dtplyr chunks that call `data.table::as.data.table()` are behind this
# guard and need none of their own, dtplyr importing data.table.
has_dtplyr <- marginplyr_suggest_available("dtplyr")
has_arrow <- marginplyr_suggest_available("arrow")
```

## Backend support matrix

One row per backend family; the sections below give each cell's detail.

| Backend | Summary | Expansion | Shares | Nesting | `where()` in `.by` or `.grouping` | Factor dimension | Sent while a call is built |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DuckDB | Native `GROUPING SETS`, except the calls listed under *Portable fallback SQL* | `UNION ALL` over one materialized read of the input | Computed | Refused | Accepted | Kept as an `ENUM`; an ordered factor returns unordered | A catalog query and a zero-row read; the share question once per R session |
| PostgreSQL | Native `GROUPING SETS`, except the calls listed under *Portable fallback SQL* | `UNION ALL` over one read of the input | Computed | Refused | Refused | Text | The share question once per R session |
| SQLite | Portable `UNION ALL` | `UNION ALL`; a live connection reads the input once into a materialized common table expression | Refused unless `.check_share_source = FALSE` | Refused | Refused | Text | The share question once per R session |
| Other SQL dialects | Portable `UNION ALL` | `UNION ALL`, one read of the input per grouping set | Computed where the dialect refuses an ineligible source; otherwise refused unless `.check_share_source = FALSE` | Refused | Refused | Text | The share question once per R session on a live connection; nothing on a simulated one |
| Arrow | Lazy, one read of the input per grouping set | Lazy, over one in-memory copy of the input | Refused | Refused | Accepted | Character under a non-missing label; kept under `NULL` or `NA_character_` | Nothing |
| dtplyr | Lazy | Lazy | Computed; the source is checked at `collect()` | `nest_with_margins()` lazy; `nest_by_with_margins()` collects | Accepted | Kept | A zero-row evaluation of the input |

*Shares* is `share_of_parent()` and `share_of_total()`. The share question
is sent only for a call that requests a share; *Parent shares use a staged
lazy query* below says what it asks. *Text* means the database stored the
factor as text before marginplyr read it, so the dimension returns as
character. Every backend also reads the input when
`.check_margin_label = TRUE` asks for the observed label check. A converted
dimension's text is the backend's own; see *Converted dimension text* below.

Support is not one status. SQL simulation is useful evidence about rendering,
but it is not the same as running a query on a live server, so treat a
simulator-only backend as SQL-generation support, and report server-specific
behavior with a minimal query and the backend version. Which claim rests on
which is stated in one place: *Database backend coverage* in the
[`margin_verbs` reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html#database-backend-coverage).

### Converted dimension text

With a character `.margin_label`, the default, a Margin dimension — a
column `.grouping` selects, which a grouping set can omit to form a margin —
that is not a factor becomes character so that it can hold the label. On a lazy input
that text is the backend's own cast, so it is not always the text a local
result holds:

| Dimension | Local and dtplyr | DuckDB | SQLite | Arrow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| double `10` | `"10"` | `"10.0"` | `"10.0"` | `"10"` |
| logical `TRUE` | `"TRUE"` | `"true"` | `"1"` | `"true"` |
| Date `2024-01-01` | `"2024-01-01"` | `"2024-01-01"` | `"19723.0"` | `"2024-01-01"` |
| integer `10` | `"10"` | `"10"` | `"10"` | `"10"` |

So `filter(year == "2024")` over a double `year` matches nothing on DuckDB,
and a join on such a key between a local result and a database one matches
nothing either. When the text matters, give the column the type or text you
want with `mutate()` before the Margin verb; for a whole-number double,
`as.integer()` is enough, since an integer's text is the same everywhere. To
keep every dimension's type instead, set `.margin_label = NULL` or
`NA_character_`, which marks margin rows with a missing value and converts
nothing on any backend.

## One report, two execution locations

The local report uses store detail, region subtotals, and a company total:

```{r}
january_sales <- retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan")

local_result <- january_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    level = grouping_id(region, store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  arrange(region, store)

local_result
```

The Grouping specification does not change when the input becomes a lazy
table. Both calls write `na.rm = TRUE` so that their results match: locally a
missing measure makes every subtotal and total that includes it `NA`, while a
SQL aggregate always drops missing values, and dbplyr warns when
`na.rm = TRUE` is absent:

```{r}
postgres_sales <- dbplyr::tbl_lazy(
  january_sales,
  con = dbplyr::simulate_postgres()
)

postgres_query <- postgres_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    level = grouping_id(region, store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  arrange(region, store)
```

`postgres_query` is still lazy. `show_query()` inspects the query without
collecting the result:

```{r}
show_query(postgres_query)
```

Use `show_query()` during interactive analysis. Use
`dbplyr::sql_render()` when code needs the rendered SQL value for logging,
testing, or another programmatic purpose.

Building a Margin query never reads your table's rows. Rows are read when you
execute the query, with `collect()`, `compute()`, or a printed preview, and
when you ask marginplyr, with `.check_margin_label = TRUE`, to look for an
observed label: a source value equal to the Margin label. Building the query
may still send internal queries that read no source values; *When marginplyr
queries your data* in the
[`margin_verbs` reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html#when-marginplyr-queries-your-data)
enumerates them, and *Record the SQL marginplyr prepares* below shows how to
see them. The one exception is `nest_by_with_margins()` on dtplyr, described
under *Other lazy backends*.

## Native grouping sets

Summaries on DuckDB and PostgreSQL use marginplyr's native path; *Portable
fallback SQL* below states what uses the other one. The generated query
contains one `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS` operation. The requested rollup:

```text
(region, store)
(region)
()
```

becomes the equivalent SQL grouping-set list. In SQL, `GROUPING(x)` returns `1`
when `x` was removed from the grouping set that produced a row and `0` when it
remained part of the group. marginplyr adds one such flag per dimension and
keeps it out of the result, so the outer query labels only the dimensions
aggregation removed. A source `NULL` therefore stays different from a generated
subtotal even though SQL would otherwise display both as missing.

More complex Grouping specifications use the same translation. The two
rollups below are combined by Cartesian product, matching comma-separated SQL
`GROUP BY` items:

```{r}
dbplyr::tbl_lazy(
  retail_sales,
  con = dbplyr::simulate_postgres()
) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    .grouping = grouping_spec(
      rollup(year, month),
      rollup(region, store)
    )
  ) |>
  show_query()
```

`grouping_sets(rollup(...), rollup(...))` has different semantics: it forms
the union of two independent hierarchies. See [Get
started](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/get_started.html#union-versus-cartesian-product)
for the complete comparison.

## Execute in DuckDB

The simulator above verifies SQL rendering without a server. DuckDB lets the
same workflow execute against a live in-memory database:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

# `shared_home = FALSE` keeps DuckDB's extension cache and stored secrets in
# the session's temporary directory rather than in `~/.duckdb`.
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))

sales_db <- copy_to(
  con,
  retail_sales,
  name = "retail_sales",
  temporary = TRUE,
  overwrite = TRUE
)

duckdb_query <- sales_db |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan") |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    level = grouping_id(region, store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  arrange(region, store)

show_query(duckdb_query)
```

At this point `duckdb_query` is still lazy. `collect()` asks DuckDB to execute
the grouping sets and transfers only the summarized result:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

duckdb_result <- collect(duckdb_query)
duckdb_result
```

The `arrange()` above orders by the labels, so `"Total"` falls wherever that
string does among a dimension's values. `.sort` orders by the structure of the
Grouping plan instead, so each subtotal lands with the rows it summarizes. It
is an argument of the verb rather than a step after it; *Margin order* in the
[`margin_verbs` reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html#margin-order)
states the key it builds and what a later verb can do to it:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

sales_db |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan") |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  collect()
```

The order survives a later verb only when dbplyr folds that verb into the same
query. On DuckDB it is kept through `filter()`, `head()`, `rename()`,
`distinct()`, and a `select()` that keeps every grouping column. It is dropped
by `mutate()`, `transmute()`, a `select()` that drops a grouping column, and a
join, each of which reads the ordered query as a subquery; dbplyr then warns
that *ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT*. A `count()`, `tally()`,
or `summarise()` either drops it the same way or is folded into the ordered
query itself, which keeps its `ORDER BY` over columns the aggregate no longer
groups by, and DuckDB and PostgreSQL refuse that statement with an error such
as *column ... must appear in the GROUP BY clause*; which of the two happens
depends on how dbplyr folds the query. So `collect()` first and continue
locally, aggregate a result requested with `.sort = "none"`, or call
`arrange()` last with a key you write: [Sort the newest year
first](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/recipes.html#sort-the-newest-year-first)
gives the key, and [Pivot a lazy result after
collecting](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/recipes.html#pivot-a-lazy-result-after-collecting)
and [The same join against a lazy
table](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/recipes.html#the-same-join-against-a-lazy-table)
work it through for a pivot and a join.

Use `compute()` instead of `collect()` when the next stage should remain in the
database. It executes the query and stores the result there as a remote table,
so what reads it afterwards is still a lazy query against the connection:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

duckdb_stage <- compute(duckdb_query)
class(duckdb_stage)

duckdb_stage |>
  filter(level == 1L) |>
  collect()
```

On SQLite, direct `compute()` of a Margin result has a contract of its own,
stated under [*SQLite
materialization*](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/summarize_with_margins.html#sqlite-materialization)
in the `summarize_with_margins()` reference.

Once the database holds any macro you defined, an input that calls one of
DuckDB's own scalar macros, such as `nullif()`, is refused too, even when it
never calls yours: your macro could replace a name inside their bodies, so
marginplyr cannot rule out source work hidden in the input. Call
`compute()` on the input first, and the Margin verb reads the stored table
instead. *When marginplyr queries your data* in the [`margin_verbs`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html#when-marginplyr-queries-your-data)
states the full rule.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

DuckDB also preserves factor grouping columns represented as enums. When a
factor dimension uses `.margin_label = NA_character_` or `NULL`, marginplyr
leaves the omitted dimension as a typed SQL `NULL`; it never attempts to add
an NA enum label. A non-missing label is added as an enum level and is placed
last by default or first with `.margin_label_position = "first"`.

## `.check_margin_label` on lazy inputs

Lazy inputs default to `.check_margin_label = FALSE`, and what that default
gives up is not free: an *observed* collision — a real value already in the
data equal to `.margin_label` — goes undetected, so the result carries one
row for that value and one row for the margin, and neither the row itself nor
code reading the result afterward can tell which is which. *When marginplyr
queries your data* in the [`margin_verbs`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html#when-marginplyr-queries-your-data)
states the rule this default follows. `nest_by_with_margins()` reads a
`dtplyr` step's rows when called, so it checks one by default.

Two protections hold at no added query. The first applies wherever marginplyr
holds factor-level metadata.

A label equal to a *declared* factor level is rejected there, because the
level is already known from the column's metadata and finding the collision
reads nothing. The enum preservation above is what makes this visible on
DuckDB: `region` below declares `"Total"` as an unused level, and
`.margin_label = "Total"` is rejected before the result query is built, even
though `.check_margin_label` is left at its lazy default:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
region_data <- data.frame(
  region = factor(c("East", "West"), levels = c("East", "West", "Total")),
  revenue = c(10, 20)
)
region_db <- copy_to(
  con,
  region_data,
  name = "region_data",
  temporary = TRUE,
  overwrite = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: declared-level-rejected
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb
#| error: true
#| purl: false

region_db |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    total = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region)
  )
```

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

Arrow is different. A factor Margin dimension there returns as character,
so Arrow does not expose its declared levels to this check; see *Arrow
inputs* in the [`margin_verbs`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html#arrow-inputs).
An unused declared level therefore does not make two result rows look alike.
An observed collision still does, and `.check_margin_label = TRUE` rejects it.

Keeping `grouping_bit()` or `grouping_id()` in the result is the other free
protection: either identifies every margin row structurally, so a source row
and a margin row that print alike still differ in a column you can read,
whatever `.check_margin_label` finds or misses.

Opt into `.check_margin_label = TRUE` when that query is worth its cost for
your backend and workload: it scans every input row of the checked columns.

## Portable fallback SQL

marginplyr emits native `GROUPING SETS` only for summaries on the DuckDB and
PostgreSQL dialects, and no option requests it elsewhere. Everything else uses
a portable query that joins one branch per grouping set with `UNION ALL`:

- every other SQL dialect, even where the database itself supports
  `GROUPING SETS`; Redshift, Snowflake, SQL Server, Oracle, Spark SQL, and
  MySQL all receive the portable query;
- a `.duplicates = "keep"` summary on PostgreSQL, and on DuckDB when it also
  names `.id` or computes a share, since each occurrence then has to be
  numbered;
- a summary that places a Grouping helper inside an aggregate, such as
  `sum(grouping_bit(region) * revenue)`, or inside a function dbplyr passes
  to the database untranslated;
- every `expand_with_margins()` call, DuckDB and PostgreSQL included.

How often the portable query reads its input depends on the verb and the
backend:

- A summary reads the source once per grouping set. On every dialect except
  DuckDB and PostgreSQL it also begins with a branch that returns zero rows,
  `WHERE (0)` on SQLite below, that exists only to fix the result's column
  types, so the three-set rollup below names `` `df` `` four times. On a live
  SQLite connection, `.sort` adds one more zero-row branch.
- An expansion on DuckDB, PostgreSQL, or a live SQLite 3.35 or later
  connection reads its input once into a common table expression, which
  DuckDB and SQLite are told to materialize and PostgreSQL materializes
  because every branch references it. The cost there is one materialized copy
  of the input rather than one scan per set; SQLite still adds a zero-row
  branch over the source.
- An expansion on any other connection, including the SQLite simulator below,
  reads the source once per grouping set after the zero-row branch, and SQLite
  adds a second zero-row branch.

A branch that reads the source repeats the input's whole lazy pipeline: on
SQLite, a filtered and joined input under a `cube()` of two dimensions renders
its join five times. The number of branches grows with the plan, and a
`cube()` of n dimensions is 2^n grouping sets. Every path except a native
summary builds one branch per grouping set in your R session before the
database sees the query: a summary of 4,096 grouping sets on a near-empty
SQLite table took over two minutes to build and collect. A Grouping plan of
more than 4,096 grouping sets is therefore refused on every backend unless
`options(marginplyr.max_grouping_sets = )` raises the limit; see
[Grouping specifications from user input](#grouping-specifications-from-user-input).
Inspect the database's query plan for large workloads; marginplyr does not
claim that either translation is universally faster.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_sqlite_simulator

sqlite_sales <- dbplyr::tbl_lazy(
  january_sales,
  con = dbplyr::simulate_sqlite()
)

sqlite_query <- sqlite_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    level = grouping_id(region, store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

show_query(sqlite_query)
```

This SQL is longer than the native form, but it preserves the same requested
grouping levels and Margin labels. Which of the two translations runs is
chosen from the connection's SQL dialect; analysis code does not need a
different Grouping specification.

`expand_with_margins()` also stays lazy, and on every backend its SQL makes
the row-expansion branches explicit. On the SQLite simulator,
`expand_with_margins(sqlite_sales, .grouping = rollup(region, store))` renders
two zero-row branches that fix the column types, then one branch per grouping
set, each reading `` `df` `` and writing `'Total'` into the dimensions its set
omits, all joined by `UNION ALL`.

## Grouping specifications from user input

A `cube()` doubles with each column it selects, so a selection helper reaches
a large plan without naming a column. On a table with 13 flag columns,
`cube(starts_with("flag_"))` asks for 8,192 grouping sets, more than the
limit of 4,096, and is refused before a branch is built:

```{r}
#| label: grouping-plan-limit-rejected
#| error: true
#| purl: false

flags <- as.data.frame(
  stats::setNames(as.list(rep("y", 13)), paste0("flag_", 1:13))
)
inspect_grouping(flags, .grouping = cube(starts_with("flag_")))
```

An application that passes its user's column choice into a Grouping
specification, as in `cube(all_of(chosen))`, cannot rely on the limit to make
that safe. At 4,096 grouping sets a summary still takes minutes to build on
the backends that build one branch per set, an expansion returns one copy of
every input row per set, and a portable summary reads its source once per
set. What bounds the call is the application limiting how many columns can be
chosen, the database's own limits, such as a statement timeout, a memory limit
or a billing cap, and `setTimeLimit()` around the call. A time limit ends the
call with an error, but not always with the time-limit message: where it
strikes inside dplyr, dplyr's own error can arrive instead. Handle any error
from the call rather than matching the message:

```{r}
#| eval: false

# `expr` is evaluated after the limit is set, and the limit is lifted
# however the call ends.
within_time_limit <- function(expr, seconds) {
  setTimeLimit(elapsed = seconds, transient = TRUE)
  on.exit(setTimeLimit(elapsed = Inf))
  expr
}

report <- tryCatch(
  within_time_limit(
    summarize_with_margins(
      sales,
      revenue = sum(revenue),
      .grouping = cube(all_of(chosen))
    ),
    seconds = 30
  ),
  error = function(cnd) NULL
)
```

## Record the SQL marginplyr prepares

A call's record has two kinds of row. Its internal rows are what marginplyr
sent while building the call; its `"result"` row is what your `collect()` will
send.

`show_query()` displays only the result query. To see the internal rows too,
set `options(marginplyr.audit_sql = TRUE)` **before** the Margin verb call or
`inspect_grouping()` call, then read them with
`last_sent_queries(include_result = FALSE)`:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

old <- options(marginplyr.audit_sql = TRUE)

audit_con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
audit_sales <- copy_to(
  audit_con,
  january_sales,
  name = "january_sales",
  temporary = TRUE,
  overwrite = TRUE
)

audit_query <- audit_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .check_margin_label = TRUE
  )

internal <- last_sent_queries(include_result = FALSE)
internal$purpose
writeLines(internal$sql[!is.na(internal$sql)])
```

The first row is DuckDB's catalog query, and the last is the observed Margin
label check that `.check_margin_label = TRUE` requested: it scans every input
row of the checked columns and retrieves one row, with one collision count per
checked column. Recording sends no query of its own.

Each `purpose` names why a row was recorded. Only `"result"` is stable; the
other names describe today's internal work and may change:

- `"result"`: the query the verb returns, rendered but not executed.
- `"relation_catalog"`: DuckDB's catalog query, checking that the input hides
  no source work behind a view or macro.
- `"selection_proxy"`: the zero-row read of the input that recovers column
  types and factor levels.
- `"observed_label_collision"`: the label check `.check_margin_label = TRUE`
  requests.
- `"share_dialect"`: the table-free question a contextual share —
  `share_of_parent()` or `share_of_total()` — asks, whether the dialect
  refuses a summary that is not a number.
- `"share_dialect_control"`: the numeric query sent after that question
  raised, confirming the connection could be asked at all.
- `"share_dialect_transaction"`: on RPostgres within a caller's transaction,
  a savepoint statement isolating those two questions.

The default view adds the `"result"` row, the SQL that `collect(audit_query)`
then executes:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

sent <- last_sent_queries()
writeLines(sent$sql[sent$purpose == "result"])
```

This is the guide's first share request on DuckDB, so it sends the dialect
question; DuckDB rejects the string aggregate, and the numeric control
follows. A later share request reuses the answer and records neither row:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

share_query <- summarize_with_margins(
  audit_sales, revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
  share = share_of_total(revenue), .grouping = rollup(region)
)
last_sent_queries(include_result = FALSE)["purpose"]
```

`details = TRUE` adds each row's `source`, `status`, and captured
`conditions`. The [`last_sent_queries()` reference][sent-queries] defines
them and states what the record promises: what replaces it, what a failed call
leaves, and what an empty view means. *When marginplyr queries your data* in
the [`margin_verbs` reference][shared-reference] enumerates the operations and
applicable backends.

[sent-queries]: https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/last_sent_queries.html
[shared-reference]: https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html#when-marginplyr-queries-your-data

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

DBI::dbDisconnect(audit_con)
options(old)
```

## Parent shares use a staged lazy query

`share_of_parent()` needs a denominator from another grouping-set row, so it
cannot be translated as one ordinary aggregate expression. marginplyr first
computes the ordinary summaries for every grouping set, then builds one
denominator lookup — the parent row for each result row — shared by every
requested measure. `.check_share_source = FALSE` appears here because
the simulated connection executes nothing, so it cannot be asked how its
dialect treats an ineligible share source.

```{r}
parent_query <- postgres_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    revenue_share = share_of_parent(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .check_share_source = FALSE
  )

show_query(parent_query)
```

This is still one lazy query. `show_query()` renders it without execution;
only an explicit operation such as `collect()` or `compute()` asks the backend
to run it. Native and portable grouping adapters both feed the same staged
Parent-share contract. Parent matching uses internal Grouping identity and
missing-safe keys rather than displayed Margin labels; [Parent lookup is
structural](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/grouping_identity.html#parent-lookup-is-structural)
works that through.

`share_of_total()` stages the same way. Its denominator depends on the fixed
`.by` keys and nothing else. Both helpers use window functions over the staged
SQL summaries, so a share agrees with its displayed denominator even for a
stateful or nondeterministic source summary. A dialect without window support,
such as Access, reports an unsupported operation when rendering or executing
the query; explicitly collect its input first to request local shares.

*Lazy execution boundaries* in the
[`share_of_parent()` reference][share-boundaries] states how each dialect
treats a share source of the wrong type and what `.check_share_source = FALSE`
changes. marginplyr reads no row of your data to learn which a dialect does:
it asks, with at most two queries referencing none of your tables. DuckDB
refuses an ineligible source itself, so on a live DuckDB table the diagnostic
is DuckDB's own, and the column it names carries the name of the summary to
rewrite. The remedy is an explicit conversion to a
number in that ordinary summary:

[share-boundaries]: https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/share_of_parent.html#lazy-execution-boundaries
[share-reference]: https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/share_of_parent.html

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

sample_con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
sample_sales <- copy_to(
  sample_con,
  january_sales,
  name = "january_sales",
  temporary = TRUE,
  overwrite = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: duckdb-ineligible-share-source
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb
#| error: true
#| purl: false

sample_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    last_channel = max(channel, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_channel_share = share_of_parent(last_channel),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  collect()
```

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

DBI::dbDisconnect(sample_con)
```

The dialect's answer settles the case once per R session and is reused for
every later connection carrying that dialect. A question left unanswered — a
dropped connection, a permissions failure, a dialect whose SQL scaffolding
the question lacks, or a query that could not be built against the
connection — refuses the share the same way, but nothing about it is
remembered, so the next share request asks again. Inside a transaction begun
through DBI with RPostgres, a savepoint isolates the two questions; up to four
transaction control statements preserve earlier work, leave commit or
rollback to you, read none of your tables, and are recorded by
`last_sent_queries()` as `share_dialect_transaction` rows.

A dialect is asked about type alone; *[Lazy execution
boundaries][share-boundaries]* says which summary that is not one value per
grouping row is detected. On DuckDB and PostgreSQL the result query checks a
bare, single-argument `UNNEST()` at the top level of a direct `dbplyr::sql()`
share source, such as `SUM(amount) + UNNEST(ARRAY[10])`: an array of zero or
more than one element causes a database error on execution. The check recognizes SQL expressions
with standard quotes and without comments. Any other direct SQL source must
itself return one value per grouping row; unless the database refuses it, one
that returns several or none is not detected.

With `.check_share_source = FALSE` on live SQLite, a direct `collect()` keeps
a declared double share when the result is empty or a finite prefix contains
only missing shares; *SQLite materialization* in the
[`summarize_with_margins()`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/summarize_with_margins.html#sqlite-materialization)
covers direct `compute()`.

The [`share_of_parent()` reference][share-reference] states both helpers'
supported sources, value rules, `across()` forms, and empty inputs.

## Completion stays in the lazy input pipeline

marginplyr does not create absent dimension keys or move completion data
between R and a database. Use a same-connection dimension relation, or move a
local relation explicitly before the Margin operation. The [Complete absent
keys before margins
guide](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/completing_keys.html)
shows a lazy dimension-table union and join, `dbplyr::copy_inline()` for small
local keys, and explicit `dplyr::copy_to()` for larger or reusable keys.

## Other lazy backends

dtplyr is lazy without being a SQL connection: the Margin verb returns a
lazy step, and `collect()` runs the data.table code it built:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_dtplyr

dt_query <- january_sales |>
  dtplyr::lazy_dt() |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

collect(dt_query)
```

Loading dtplyr does not attach data.table, but a session that also calls
`library(data.table)` after marginplyr gets data.table's `rollup()` and
`cube()` in place of marginplyr's. The call above is then refused with an
error naming `data.table::rollup()`. Write `marginplyr::rollup()` and
`marginplyr::cube()`, or attach marginplyr last.

A derived dtplyr step can compute column types or factor levels from its source
values. A request for zero output rows can still run that upstream calculation
over every source row before discarding them. marginplyr therefore reads the
types only of steps whose output types follow from their input types alone:
`filter()`, `select()`, `rename()`, `relocate()`, `arrange()`, `slice()`,
`head()`, `distinct()`, `tidyr::drop_na()`, a join whose keys are plain
logical, integer, double or character columns of the same type on both sides,
and a `transmute()` or a `mutate()` directly on `lazy_dt()` that adds
constants, column copies, or arithmetic on numeric columns. Any other step is
refused before processing source rows, including an aggregate such as
`summarise()` or `count()`, a join on a `Date` or factor key, and a `mutate()`
that calls another function:

```{r}
#| label: dtplyr-unsafe-metadata
#| eval: !expr has_dtplyr
#| error: true
#| purl: false

january_sales |>
  dtplyr::lazy_dt() |>
  mutate(region = factor(region, levels = unique(region))) |>
  inspect_grouping(.grouping = rollup(where(is.factor)))
```

Either remedy runs the step's upstream operations now. `collect()` it and pass
the resulting data frame, or stay in data.table: materialize the step with
`data.table::as.data.table()` and wrap the table in `lazy_dt()` again, which
gives the Margin verb a root whose types it can read:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_dtplyr

january_sales |>
  dtplyr::lazy_dt() |>
  mutate(region = factor(region, levels = unique(region))) |>
  data.table::as.data.table() |>
  dtplyr::lazy_dt() |>
  inspect_grouping(.grouping = rollup(where(is.factor)))
```

The step has to be built with `immutable = TRUE`, which is what `lazy_dt()`
does by default. A Margin verb builds one branch per grouping set from the
step it is given, and when the step was built with `immutable = FALSE`
data.table writes every one of those branches back to your own table by
reference. That returns a result in which each row carries the Margin label,
and leaves you holding a table that has lost a column or had its names
permuted. Such an input is refused before any branch is built:

```{r}
#| label: mutable-dtplyr-step
#| eval: !expr has_dtplyr
#| error: true
#| purl: false

data.table::as.data.table(january_sales) |>
  dtplyr::lazy_dt(immutable = FALSE) |>
  expand_with_margins(.grouping = rollup(region, store))
```

`nest_with_margins()` also supports dtplyr and remains lazy until collection.
SQL database and Arrow tables cannot use the nesting verbs because their
result contains a list column:

```{r}
#| label: nesting-a-sql-table
#| error: true
#| purl: false

postgres_sales |>
  nest_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )
```

`nest_by_with_margins()` is the row-wise counterpart. On dtplyr it is the one
Margin verb that collects a lazy input without being asked: a row-wise data
frame is a local object, so it has nothing lazy to return. Its own *dtplyr
inputs* section in the [`nest_by_with_margins()`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/nest_by_with_margins.html#dtplyr-inputs)
states this. Its detail tables are the ones dtplyr built, so each cell is a
`data.table`:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_dtplyr

january_sales |>
  dtplyr::lazy_dt() |>
  nest_by_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  mutate(revenue = sum(data$revenue))
```

dtplyr also enforces the contextual-share source rules, for `share_of_parent()`
and `share_of_total()` alike. A valid request stays a native lazy query, and an
ineligible source type or a non-scalar summary raises a marginplyr error at
explicit execution, before an invalid grouping row is emitted:

```{r}
#| label: dtplyr-ineligible-share-source
#| eval: !expr has_dtplyr
#| error: true
#| purl: false

january_sales |>
  dtplyr::lazy_dt() |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    last_channel = max(channel),
    last_channel_share = share_of_parent(last_channel),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  collect()
```

Arrow summaries and expansions are supported and lazy wherever Arrow can
evaluate the summary itself. An Arrow summary reads its source once per
grouping set, a Dataset included. An expansion of more than one grouping set
instead reads its input into one in-memory Arrow Table when it is consumed, and
every branch reads that copy. Two things are refused, for two unrelated
reasons.

The first is a summary Arrow's own engine cannot evaluate. Arrow answers one of
those by reading the whole input — every column, not just the ones the summary
names — and computing it in R, so marginplyr refuses it before a row is read:

```{r}
#| label: arrow-absorbed-summary
#| eval: !expr has_arrow
#| error: true
#| purl: false

arrow::arrow_table(january_sales) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    channels = paste(sort(unique(channel)), collapse = "/"),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )
```

*Arrow inputs* in the [`margin_verbs`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html#arrow-inputs) states
which expressions this reaches, the rewrites the diagnostic names, and what an
Arrow dataset answers instead.

The second is contextual shares. `share_of_parent()` and `share_of_total()` are
both rejected outright, before any Arrow query is constructed: marginplyr
cannot check that a share's source is a numeric scalar before Arrow builds the
query. Collect the input first, or drop the share.

```{r}
#| label: arrow-parent-share
#| eval: !expr has_arrow
#| error: true
#| purl: false

arrow::arrow_table(january_sales) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    revenue_share = share_of_parent(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: arrow-total-share
#| eval: !expr has_arrow
#| error: true
#| purl: false

arrow::arrow_table(january_sales) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    revenue_of_total = share_of_total(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )
```

The
[`share_of_parent()` reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/share_of_parent.html)
states where each backend reports these errors.

### Which Arrow inputs are supported

Arrow's tabular dplyr inputs and marginplyr's verb-specific contract are:

| Input | Summary or expansion | Inspection | Nesting |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Table`, `RecordBatch`, or `Dataset` | Accepted | Accepted | Refused; collect first |
| Query with no reader source | Accepted | Accepted | Refused; collect first |
| `RecordBatchReader` | Refused; materialize first | Accepted | Refused; collect first |
| Query with any reader source | Refused; materialize first | Accepted | Refused; collect first |
| Non-tabular Arrow object | General input refusal | General input refusal | General input refusal |

A query is judged by its complete source graph, so its class alone does not
tell you which row applies.

`RecordBatchReader` is one-pass, while a Margin operation may build one branch
per grouping set. Summary and expansion therefore refuse both a direct reader
and a query whose source graph contains one. Use `arrow::as_arrow_table()` to
consume every batch once and make the reusable table explicit.
`inspect_grouping()` executes no branch, so it accepts a direct reader or a
reader-backed query without consuming either. A direct reader is normalized to
the same unexecuted query internally:

```r
inspect_grouping(reader, .grouping = rollup(region, store))
```

For a nesting verb, collect the reader or query directly: an Arrow table still
cannot carry the list-column result. Collection changes `.check_margin_label`'s
default from `FALSE` to `TRUE`, so choose that policy explicitly on the re-run.
A `Scanner` is not a dplyr input either:
choose `$ToTable()` or `$ToRecordBatchReader()` first. Neither are `Scalar`, `Array`,
`ChunkedArray`, `Schema`, `Field`, `DataType`, or other non-tabular Arrow
objects. Convert those to a data frame or lazy dplyr table appropriate to the
data they represent.

## Practical rules for remote analysis

- Build the complete lazy pipeline before calling `collect()`.

- Use `show_query()` to confirm native `GROUPING SETS` or fallback
  `UNION ALL`.

- Use `.by` for columns that remain fixed in every grouping level.

- Keep `grouping_bit()` or `grouping_id()` when source missing values or the
  literal label `"Total"` can occur in the data.

- Lazy results have no guaranteed order unless the query explicitly requests
  one. Ask for a Margin order with `.sort`, or call `arrange()` for any other
  presentation order. A later `mutate()`, join, or aggregate drops a Margin
  order, so `collect()` first or `arrange()` last; see *Execute in DuckDB*
  above.

- Lazy inputs default to `.check_margin_label = FALSE`; see
  *`.check_margin_label` on lazy inputs* above.

- A contextual share may need `.check_share_source = FALSE`; see *Parent
  shares use a staged lazy query* above.

- A portable `UNION ALL` query can repeat the input's lazy pipeline in every
  branch; see *Portable fallback SQL* above. Where it does, `compute()` a
  filtered or joined input, or pre-aggregate it to the finest grouping set,
  before the Margin verb. The branches then read that one table, and the
  collected result is the same.
